proxy_language: Middle Korean (15th-16th c., Hunmin jeongeum/Hangul-era Korean), with Late Old Korean/Silla-Goryeo onomastic layer for court and place names; Sino-Korean vocabulary for official and ritual terms
proxy_rationale: 'Dùnbuldach' is not a known historical polity, so the culture is treated as a fictional later court (index 5) located in the China/Korea/Japan region. The only region-appropriate, richly attested and standardly transliterated language that fits a 'later court' is Korean of the Goryeo-Joseon court. Middle Korean is chosen because it is well documented in Hangul with a scholarly Yale romanization. The name's -buldach shape (b-l-d-ch clusters) does NOT fit Korean phonotactics, so the proxy link to the culture name itself is weak; Japanese (Old/Classical Japanese) is the second-best alternative. No Mongolic/Altaic claim is made beyond known loanwords such as Middle Korean mwul 'horse-related' Mongol loans (baturu, 'hero').
phonology: Middle Korean consonants (Yale-style romanization): plain stops p t c k; aspirated ph th ch kh; tense/glottalized stops (written with doubled letters, pp tt cc kk, ss) as a Hunmin jeongeum-era sibilant/tensed series; fricatives s, z (the lost 'zero' consonant), h; nasals m n ng; liquid l; glide y, w; also lost sounds such as bilabial fricative (written W/β, as in the 'pelicanized' spelling) that can be ignored in a game. Vowels: i, e, a, o, wu, u, and the lost vowel o (Middle Korean arae-a, written ʌ). Tone: Middle Korean had a pitch-accent system (low, high, rising), marked in Hunmin-era texts by dots; this is not written in game names. Vowel harmony (yang vowels a, o, ʌ vs. yin vowels e, wu, u; i neutral) governs suffixes.
phonotactics: Syllable shape (C)V(C), with only a single onset consonant and a single coda consonant, i.e. no onset or coda clusters inside one syllable. Medial clusters occur across syllable boundaries. Word-initial liquid l/r is avoided in native words (and l is restricted from word-initial position by Initial Law, 'dueum beopcik'). Codas are neutralized to p, t, k, m, n, ng, l (and s in Middle Korean). No consonant sequence like bld, dch, nbl exists inside a syllable. Native roots are typically 1-3 syllables; Sino-Korean morphemes are always one syllable (CV, CVC, CVN).
orthography: Use Revised Romanization of Korean for readability in game names: g, k, kk, n, d, t, tt, r/l, m, b, p, pp, s, ss, ng, j, jj, ch, h; vowels a, eo, o, u, eu, i, e, ae, oe, wi, ya, yeo, yo, yu, ye, yae, wa, wo, we; hyphen allowed between syllable-blocks in compounds (e.g. Dae-gwang). Scholarly alternatives are McCune-Reischauer or Yale; the audit uses Revised Romanization.
morphology: Agglutinative, strictly suffixing, SOV, head-final. Nouns are uninflected for number or gender; a plural suffix -deul (Middle Korean -tolh) is optional. Case/particles are suffixed: nominative -i/-ga, topic -eun/-neun, genitive -ui (Middle Korean -ay/-uy; with also -s), locative -e, -eseo, instrumental -ro/-euro, accusative -eul/-reul. Verbs take stacked suffixes (honorific -si-, tense, mood, connective -go, -eo). Nominalizers include -gi, -eum/-m; adjectival -n/-eun, -l. Two lexical strata are productive: native Korean and Sino-Korean (Chinese-origin morphemes, usually two-syllable binomes) with Sino-Korean dominating titles, institutions, temples, courts and administration.
compounding: Compounds are head-final: modifier + head (N+N). Native compounds may insert sai-siot, a linking s/t (e.g. bam-s-bi 'night rain'), written as sai-siot in Hangul; in Revised Romanization it is often omitted or appears as a doubled tense consonant. 'X of Y' is Y-ui X (genitive) or simply Y + X as a bare compound; 'maker of Y' is Y + maker-noun such as -jang (artisan, Sino) or -ssi/-kkun (agent; native -kkun 'person who does'). Sino-Korean binomes are formed by two nouns, verb-object (object first? No: verb-object order in Chinese, e.g. gae-guk 'found country') or modifier-head; place names often end in -san 'mountain', -gang 'river', -ju 'province', -seong 'fortress', -sa 'temple', -jeon 'hall', -gung 'palace'. Reduplication is used for sound-symbolic and onomatopoeic adverbs (ttak-ttak).
noun_phrase_order: Modifier before head throughout. Genitive/possessor precedes possessed (Y-ui X); adjectives/relative clauses (in -n/-eun, -l form) precede the noun; demonstratives and numerals precede the noun, numeral + classifier (hana, dul, set; or Sino numerals il, i, sam + classifier). Titles follow the personal name (Hong Gil-dong ssi, X-wang 'king X'; surname precedes given name).

notes: Dùnbuldach is not Korean-looking; names should use proxy morphology (Revised Romanization with Sino-Korean plus native stems), not the culture name's own sound shape. Keep syllables to (C)V(C) with hyphens between syllables when helpful. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word since this culture is not Goidelic.
